A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLPF research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additions in v5.

before.justification: v4 reports original neural-network connectivity experiments, including path loss and accuracy, repeated-mode comparisons, continuity checks and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v5 retains original connectivity results and adds baseline experiments, component ablations, dataset results, variance-range investigations and sharper-minimum tests.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same movement, variance correction, retraining and AngleConformal procedures. FDF layer ordering and the two-stage construction across variance spheres are also retained. The new ablations and endpoint experiments evaluate these existing procedures rather than introduce method components.

E1.justification: v5 Figure 10 adds evaluations labeled ImageNet10 for ResNet18 and DLA to the retained MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 coverage. This is a limited extension of image-classification coverage. Additional architectures evaluated on CIFAR100 extend model configurations within an existing dataset and task.

E2.justification: v4 principally provides a literature-based comparison in Table 1. v5 adds original FGE testing in Appendix C and AutoNEB comparisons using standard/fast configurations in Table 9 and CCT mode pairs in Appendix J. SPRO disappears from the summary table, but neither PDF reports an original SPRO experiment.

E3.justification: v5 introduces controlled default-seed versus changed-seed FGE tests, standard/fast AutoNEB protocols, additional CIFAR100 model configurations, a weight-decay sweep with a 4000-iteration M2O path, and relative-flatness/random-perturbation evaluations. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The existing main LLPF search schedules are retained in renumbered Tables 4–5.

E4.justification: New Appendix I tests the necessity of layer-wise movement, retraining and variance correction. Appendices J–L add an AutoNEB failure case, an investigation of reachable variance spheres and connections between sharper minima. Figures 7–8 also expand and revise the variance/mean validation. The earlier continuity and loss-tolerance checks remain.

E5.justification: The mean/standard-deviation convention remains, but v5 specifies three runs for ResNet18/DLA on CIFAR100 and single runs for other Figure 10 cases, refining v4's broad at-least-10 statement. It also reports four runs per AutoNEB configuration and uncertainty over 100 sharpness perturbation directions. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments had their run counts reduced.

E6.justification: v5 adds substantial benchmark, ablation, sharpness and baseline results. Table 9 reports AutoNEB saddle losses of 0.519–1.648 for standard runs and 1.240–4.200 for fast runs on ResNet20/CIFAR10; its LLPF row uses ResNet18, preventing a matched performance-gain interpretation. The headline ResNet18 loss bound below 0.006 in Figure 6 was already reported in v4.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 and the variance–norm derivation are retained, with the proof moving from Appendix A.8 to Appendix M. v5 Appendix L adds a formal definition of a perturbation-based sharpness profile using weight-norm-scaled random directions and mean absolute loss changes. It adds no connectivity theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—broader architecture support, consistency across random seeds and connections across training hyperparameters—remain. v5's conclusion additionally claims lower worst-case training loss than existing methods, while its abstract more categorically characterizes previous independent-mode connectivity methods as unreliable.

C2.justification: v5 removes v4's prose flat-minimum prerequisite and argues that sharper minima can also be connected, although the pseudocode still specifies flat low-loss regions. Section 6 adds interpretations involving low-loss tunnels and a qualified conjecture of full SGD-basin path-connectedness. New passages explain variance-range limits, RegNet variability and LeNet's normalization-related degradation. The training/test-loss caveat remains in Section 5.

D1.justification: v5 supplies a source-code URL where v4 promised later release. Table 6 newly specifies the 140-epoch endpoint recipe for the existing Figure 6 result and alternate learning-rate/weight-decay recipes for cross-sphere experiments. Appendices C and F add the FGE code version and commands and AutoNEB configuration references. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the underlying LLPF implementation.

R1.justification: v5 substantially revises its positioning against FGE and AutoNEB: it argues that FGE's default training script produces correlated endpoints and emphasizes unsuccessful AutoNEB runs. It also expands discussion of landscape connectivity and sharpness through works such as Kuditipudi et al., Lubana et al. and Petzka et al. This goes beyond the numerous bibliographic metadata updates.

P1.justification: The introduction, baseline discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting, and Section 6 changes from a limitations section to a discussion of landscape geometry. The appendix is reorganized into separate lettered sections with expanded explanations and model-selection rationale. These changes materially reshape the narrative despite substantial retained method text.

P2.justification: v5 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column layout and relocates algorithms and figures. Figures 7–8 become multi-model displays, appendix benchmark panels are split and expanded, and Figure 2 gains phase annotations. Numerous diagnostic figures and comparison tables are added. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v4 demonstrated many successful paths but offered little direct testing of component necessity and endpoint restrictions. v5's ablations, sharper-minimum and variance-range investigations, baseline experiments and expanded reproducibility information substantially strengthen the empirical case for LLPF. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, although comparative claims require caution: Table 9 mixes architectures and computational budgets, and the categorical FGE criticism extends beyond the default-script and limited independent-pair evidence presented.
